items.title: How many prices in a file
items.prose: Hidden tests obey every limit in the Input section. Read it before you read the story.

lines: A desk logs prices on a grid of n rows and
m columns. Each test case is one grid. Report
The first line contains t (1 ≤ t ≤ 10⁴). Each
test case starts with n and m (1 ≤ n, m ≤ 2000),
then n lines of m integers. The sum of n·m over
all test cases does not exceed 10⁶.
For each test case, print the largest price.
params.title: Problem C

items.question: What is the most prices a single input file can hold in total?

widget.accept: 1,000,000: the sum of n·m is capped

feedback.correct: The sum of $n \cdot m$ is capped at $10^6$, so one file holds at most 1,000,000 prices.
feedback.generic: Find the sentence that bounds all the test cases together, not each one.

byKey.product: You multiplied $t$ by the largest grid. The last sentence of Input caps the total across tests.
byKey.grid: That is one 2,000 by 2,000 grid. The cap on the sum of $n \cdot m$ forbids even one such grid.
byKey.tests: That is $t$, the number of test cases, not the number of prices.

explain.text: The cap on the sum of $n \cdot m$ governs the whole file, so it holds at most 1,000,000 prices. It also limits each test: a 2,000 by 2,000 grid has $4 \cdot 10^6$ cells and can never appear. So plan for $10^6$ cells in all, not for $n$ and $m$ at their own limits.

items.title: A reader for names with spaces
items.prose: The first line holds $t$. Each test case is two lines: a desk name, which may contain spaces, then that desk's P&L as one integer. There are no blank lines.
items.question: Which reader keeps every desk name whole?

options.why: You kept the first word of the name. A name such as North Desk loses its second word.
You split on every space. North Desk becomes two tokens, and each later position shifts by one.
You split on single spaces. Names still break, and the newlines stay glued to the tokens.

feedback.correct: Each line is one field, so a name keeps its spaces.
feedback.generic: Ask what each reader does with a name that holds a space.

explain.text: `split()` with no argument breaks on every space, which tears a name apart. `splitlines()` keeps each line whole, and `int` reads the P&L line. Use tokens for numbers and lines for text that holds spaces.

items.title: Two rebalancing cycles
items.prose: A fund rebalances every 84 days and a hedge book every 90 days. Both rebalanced today.
items.question: On how many of the next 10,000 days do both rebalance?

feedback.correct: Shared days are multiples of 1,260: days 1,260 to 8,820, seven in all.
feedback.generic: Shared days fall every $\operatorname{lcm}(84, 90)$ days. Find the lcm, then count its multiples.

byKey.product: You used $84 \cdot 90 = 7{,}560$ as the cycle. They share a factor of 6, so they meet every 1,260 days.
byKey.gcd: You counted multiples of 6, the gcd. A shared day is a multiple of both periods.
byKey.today: You counted today. The question asks about the next 10,000 days.
byKey.first: 1,260 is the first shared day. Count every multiple of 1,260 up to 10,000.

explain.text: Euclid gives $\gcd(84, 90) = \gcd(84, 6) = 6$, so the lcm is $84 \cdot 90 / 6 = 1260$. Shared days are 1,260, 2,520 and so on. $\lfloor 10000 / 1260 \rfloor = 7$, since $7 \cdot 1260 = 8820$ and $8 \cdot 1260 = 10080$.

items.title: Three days, six jobs
items.prose: Six jobs each take one whole day, and three days are free. A job pays only if it is done on or before its deadline day. The rule: take jobs from the best-paid down, and put each on the latest free day on or before its deadline. Skip a job with no such day.
items.question: Tap the jobs the rule keeps.

feedback.correct: A, D and E, paying £150k: D on day 3, A on day 1 and E on day 2.
feedback.generic: Work down from £60k. Put each job on the latest free day it allows.

byKey.earliest: You put each job on the earliest free day. D then takes day 1 and blocks A, so the plan pays only £120k.
byKey.deadline: You took jobs by deadline, not pay. That keeps A, C and D for £140k and misses E's £40k.
byKey.top: You kept the three best-paid jobs. A and B both need day 1, so they cannot both be done.
byKey.r1: B also needs day 1, which A, paying more, already holds.
byKey.r2: When C comes up, days 1 and 2 are taken.
byKey.r5: F comes last, and days 1 to 3 are all taken.

explain.text: D goes on day 3, A on day 1 and E on day 2, which fills the days. Taking the latest free day keeps early days for jobs with early deadlines. An exchange argument shows that no plan beats £150k.

items.title: Upsolving done properly
items.prose: Your rating is 1,250. Your upsolving log for this week has four entries.
items.question: Select all that apply: which entries count as upsolved?

options.text: G (1,400): took the idea from the editorial, closed it, coded it from scratch, accepted. Redo booked for next week.
H (1,350): solved alone after two days of thought, with a size test of $2 \cdot 10^5$ values. Redo booked for next week.
J (1,500): copied the editorial's code and got it accepted.

options.text: K (1,450): read the editorial, agreed with it and marked it solved.
options.why: Agreeing with an editorial is not solving. Code it until it is accepted, then redo it a week later.

feedback.correct: G and H were coded from scratch, accepted and booked for a redo.
feedback.generic: An upsolve counts when you wrote the accepted code yourself and booked a redo.

explain.text: Upsolving means writing an accepted solution without the editorial open. G and H do that and book a cold redo. J and K only read or copied, so the idea is not yet yours.

items.title: Emptying a list from the front
items.prose:
A replay tool drains its queued orders like this.

```python
while orders:
    orders.pop(0)
```

Each `pop(0)` shifts every entry behind the removed one a place to the left. The tool may spend at most $10^8$ shifts.
items.question: What is the largest number of queued orders it can drain within that budget?

feedback.correct: $14{,}142 \cdot 14{,}141 / 2 = 99{,}991{,}011$ shifts fits, and one more order needs 100,005,153.
feedback.generic: Draining $n$ orders costs $n(n-1)/2$ shifts. Find the largest $n$ that keeps this within $10^8$.

byKey.square: You solved $n^2 \le 10^8$. Each pop shifts only the entries left, so the total is about half that.
byKey.pops: That allows $10^8$ pops. Each pop also shifts all the entries behind it.

explain.text: With $m$ entries left, `pop(0)` shifts $m - 1$, so $n$ orders cost $n(n-1)/2$ shifts. That stays within $10^8$ up to $n = 14{,}142$, near $\sqrt{2 \cdot 10^8}$. `collections.deque` with `popleft` drains a million orders in $10^6$ steps.

items.title: Which plans fit the budget
items.prose: A C++ solution runs about $10^8$ simple steps a second, and the limit is 2 seconds. The budget is $2 \cdot 10^8$ steps. Use $\sqrt{2 \cdot 10^5} \approx 447.2$.
items.question: Fill in each plan's step count, then answer yes or no for fits.

feedback.correct: Two plans fit: $9 \cdot 10^6$ and $8.9 \cdot 10^7$. The other two need $8 \cdot 10^9$ and $8.4 \cdot 10^8$.
feedback.generic: Compute each step count at the largest input, then compare it with $2 \cdot 10^8$.

explain.text: Count the steps at the largest input, then compare with the budget. $n^3$ is out at 2,000, while $n \sqrt{n}$ fits at $2 \cdot 10^5$ with room to spare. $n \cdot 2^n$ at $n = 25$ is four times over, so it needs a better idea.

items.title: Pairs of equal P&L days
items.prose:
**Problem.** The first number is $t$, the number of test cases ($1 \le t \le 10^4$). Each test case gives $n$, then $n$ daily P&L values in whole pounds, each from $-10^9$ to $10^9$. The sum of $n$ is at most $2 \cdot 10^5$.

For each test case, print the number of pairs of days $i < j$ with equal P&L. Values may wrap over several lines, blank lines may appear, and the last line may have no newline.
items.question: Write a program that reads all of standard input and prints one answer per test case.

widget.starter:
import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
# t test cases, each: n, then n values.
# Print the number of pairs i < j with
# equal values, one line per case.
widget.solution:
import sys
from collections import Counter

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
t = int(data[0])
pos = 1
out = []
for _ in range(t):
    n = int(data[pos])
    pos += 1
    counts = Counter(map(int, data[pos:pos + n]))
    pos += n
    out.append(sum(c * (c - 1) // 2 for c in counts.values()))
print("\n".join(map(str, out)))
widget.how: Check runs your program 7 times, each with its own input. Test 3 wraps values over lines. Test 4 has blank lines and no final newline. Test 6 has 2,000 small cases. Test 7 has one case of 32,000 values. Comparing every pair, even with `list.count`, needs over $5 \cdot 10^8$ comparisons. It is stopped at the 5 s limit.

feedback.correct: Read once, count with a dict, print once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test's input.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 wraps one test case's values over two lines. Read tokens, not lines.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has blank lines, no final newline, and 7 next to −7. Split into tokens, and keep 7 and −7 apart.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has three zeros. Count every value, zero included.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 has 2,000 small cases. Check that your position moves past every value of a case.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has 32,000 values in one case. Comparing every pair is too slow; count equal values with a dict.
byKey.error: Your program stopped with an error. Read the last line of the message under the editor.

explain.text: Tokens ignore line layout, so one `read().split()` and a position cover the wrapped, blank and unterminated inputs. Equal values are grouped with a `Counter`, and a group of $c$ days gives $c(c-1)/2$ pairs. That is $O(n)$ per case instead of comparing every pair.

items.title: Dividing under a prime modulus
items.prose: Work modulo the prime 17. A check needs the whole number $x$ from 0 to 16 with $5x \equiv 3 \pmod{17}$.
items.question: What is $x$?

feedback.correct: $x = 3 \cdot 5^{-1} = 3 \cdot 7 = 21 \equiv 4$, and $5 \cdot 4 = 20 \equiv 3$.
feedback.generic: Multiply both sides by the inverse of 5 modulo 17, then reduce.

byKey.inverse: 7 is the inverse of 5, since $5 \cdot 7 = 35 \equiv 1$. You still need to multiply it by 3.
byKey.floor: You divided the remainder: $3 // 5 = 0$. Division needs the inverse of 5, not integer division.
byKey.times: You multiplied by 5: $3 \cdot 5 = 15$. But $5 \cdot 15 = 75 \equiv 7$, not 3. Multiply by the inverse of 5.

explain.text: Modulo 17 the inverse of 5 is $5^{15} \equiv 7$, because $5 \cdot 7 = 35 = 2 \cdot 17 + 1$. Then $x \equiv 3 \cdot 7 = 21 \equiv 4$. Check: $5 \cdot 4 = 20 \equiv 3$.

items.title: What the sieve has not crossed out
items.prose: A sieve lists the primes up to 60. So far it has crossed out the multiples of 2 and 3, starting at each prime's square. 1 and the crossed-out numbers are faded.
items.question: Tap every composite number still standing.

feedback.correct: 25, 35, 49 and 55: each has 5 or 7 as its smallest prime factor.
feedback.generic: A composite left over has a prime factor that has not been crossed out yet. Test each standing number.

byKey.one: 1 is not prime, but it is not composite either. Look for a product of two primes.
byKey.r5c7: 47 is prime: nothing below $\sqrt{47}$ divides it.
byKey.r6c1: 51 is divisible by 3, so it is crossed out.
byKey.fives: You found the multiples of 5. 49 is $7 \cdot 7$ and is still standing too.

explain.text: Every composite up to 60 has a prime factor at most $\sqrt{60} < 8$. After 2 and 3, the multiples of 5 from 25 and of 7 from 49 remain: 25, 35, 55 and 49. So the sieve must still process 5 and 7, and no prime above 7 is needed.

items.title: Flipping neighbouring coins
items.prose: Seven coins lie in a row, all heads. A move flips two neighbouring coins. You may make any number of moves.
items.question: Select all that apply: which quantities can no move change?

options.text: Whether the number of tails is even or odd
Whether the number of heads is even or odd

options.why: You expected the count to stay put. One move turns two heads into two tails, so it changes by 2.
You reduced modulo 4. Two heads to two tails adds 2, which changes the remainder.

options.text: Whether the leftmost coin is heads
options.why: You watched one end. Flipping coins 1 and 2 turns the leftmost coin over.

feedback.correct: Each move changes the tails count by $-2$, $0$ or $+2$, so its parity stays. Heads is 7 minus tails.
feedback.generic: A move flips two coins. Ask how the count of tails can change in one move.

explain.text: One move changes the tails count by $+2$, $0$ or $-2$, so its parity is invariant. With 7 coins, heads is $7 - \text{tails}$, so the parity of heads is invariant too. All-tails would need 7 tails, an odd number, and is unreachable.

items.title: Factorial tables in order
items.prose: We answer many queries $\binom{n}{k} \bmod p$ with $p = 10^9 + 7$ and $n \le N = 10^6$. We build two tables once, then answer in $O(1)$ each. Two of the six lines do not belong.
items.question: Put the four steps in the order that works, and leave out the two that do not belong.

lines.text: Fill `fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % p` for `i` from 1 up to `N`
Fill `ifact[i - 1] = ifact[i] * i % p` for `i` from `N` down to 1
Answer each query as `fact[n] * ifact[k] % p * ifact[n - k] % p`
Fill `ifact[i] = pow(fact[i], p - 2, p)` for every `i` from 0 to `N`
lines.why: That is one `pow` per entry, about 30 squarings each. The backward loop needs one `pow` in all.

lines.text: Fill `ifact[i + 1] = ifact[i] * (i + 1) % p` for `i` from 0 up to `N - 1`
lines.why: You ran the inverse loop forwards. Multiplying by $i + 1$ undoes a factor, so it only works downwards from `ifact[N]`.

feedback.correct: Forward factorials, one inverse, backward inverses, then queries.
feedback.generic: Each table needs the one before it. The backward loop needs a starting value.

byKey.s2: The single `pow` needs `fact[N]`, so the forward table comes first.
byKey.s3: The backward loop starts from `ifact[N]`, so the `pow` line must come before it.
byKey.s4: A query reads both tables, so it comes last.
byKey.left-out: Two lines do not belong: one `pow` per entry is slow, and the inverse loop cannot run forwards.

explain.text: `fact[N]` needs the forward loop, and one `pow` turns it into `ifact[N]`. Each earlier inverse is the next one times `i`, because each factorial gains one factor. That costs one `pow` in total, not one per entry.

items.title: Swapping two neighbouring jobs
items.prose: A desk runs four jobs one after another. Their times in minutes, in order, are 4, 9, 2, 7. A job's completion time is the minute it finishes. The desk wants the smallest total of completion times. We swap the middle two jobs, giving the order 4, 2, 9, 7.
items.question: By how much does the total of completion times fall?

feedback.correct: Before: 4, 13, 15, 22 total 54. After: 4, 6, 15, 22 total 47. The total falls by 7.
feedback.generic: Find which completion times change. Jobs outside the swapped pair end at the same minute.

byKey.longer: 9 is the time of the job that moved back. The pair's second job still ends at minute 15, so the fall is smaller.
byKey.shorter: 2 is the time of the shorter job. The first slot of the pair now ends at 6 instead of 13.
byKey.sum: You added both job times. Only the first slot of the pair finishes earlier, by $9 - 2$.

explain.text: Before the swap the pair finishes at 13 and 15, and after it at 6 and 15. The first ends $9 - 2 = 7$ sooner and the second at the same minute. A longer job before a shorter one is never better: that is the exchange argument.

items.title: Masks that avoid a trade set
items.prose: Four trades are bits 0 to 3 of a mask. The set holding trades 1 and 3 is the mask 1010, which is 10. A mask is disjoint from 1010 when the two share no trade.
items.question: Tap every mask disjoint from 1010.

feedback.correct: Four masks: 0000, 0001, 0100 and 0101, the submasks of 0101.
feedback.generic: Check each mask bit by bit: it may not have a 1 where 1010 has a 1.

byKey.sub: You tapped the submasks of 1010. Those share trades with it; disjoint masks avoid bits 1 and 3.
byKey.nonzero: You left out 0000. The empty set shares no trade with anything.
byKey.r1c3: 0010 has a 1 at bit 1, which 1010 also uses.

explain.text: A mask $m$ is disjoint from 1010 exactly when `m & 0b1010 == 0`. That makes $m$ a submask of the complement 0101, so there are $2^2 = 4$. Enumerating the submasks of the complement skips every clashing mask.

items.title: Fewest updates
items.prose: **Problem.** A fund wants its holding on days 1 to $n$ to end at `target[i]` shares, with $1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ and $0 \le$ `target[i]` $\le 10^9$. Every day starts at 0. One update adds 1 share to every day of a range $l$ to $r$. Find the fewest updates that reach the target exactly.
items.question: Complete `fewest_updates(target)`.

widget.prelude:
import random as _rnd


def _target(n, hi, seed):
    g = _rnd.Random(seed)
    return [g.randint(0, hi) for _ in range(n)]
widget.starter:
def fewest_updates(target):
    """Each update adds 1 to a range of days.
    Return the fewest updates that build target."""
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. Tests 1 to 6 are hand cases: a gap, one day, all zeros, a flat run, a dip and a peak. Test 7 is random. Tests 8 and 9 have 200,000 days. Splitting at each minimum or peeling one layer at a time is stopped at the 5 s limit.

feedback.correct: Each rise from one day to the next needs that many new updates; a fall needs none.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 has a 0 between two 2s. No update can jump the gap, so it needs 4.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 dips to 1. The rise from 1 back to 4 needs 3 new updates.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 rises on all 200,000 days. Add up the rises in one pass instead of splitting at each minimum.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 has values up to $10^9$. Peeling one layer at a time cannot finish; add up the positive differences.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Read the last line of the message under the editor.

explain.text: An update adds 1 to the difference array at day $l$ and takes 1 off after day $r$. So each positive difference of the target counts update starts, and none can be shared. The answer is the sum of $\max(0, t_i - t_{i-1})$ with $t_0 = 0$, in $O(n)$.

items.title: Reading a failing case
items.prose: Problem: count the pairs $i < j$ with $x_i + x_j = k$. Your stress loop stops at its first difference and prints it.
items.question: Which bug explains this case?

options.text: The fast code also pairs each value with itself, $i = j$
The fast code counts each pair twice, as $(i, j)$ and $(j, i)$
options.why: Counting both orders gives 2 here, not 3. Only the two 2s sum to 4.

options.text: The fast code uses `<` where it needs `<=`
options.why: This problem asks for an exact sum, so no `<` against $k$ is involved. That bug cannot add pairs.

options.text: The brute force is wrong and misses pairs
options.why: The brute force says 1, and the two 2s are the only pair summing to 4. It is right.

feedback.correct: With $i = j$ allowed, each 2 also pairs with itself, so 1 becomes 3.
feedback.generic: List every pair the fast count could have found, and see which rule gives 3.

explain.text: The true pairs are only the two 2s, so 1 is right. Allowing $i = j$ also counts each 2 with itself, since $2 + 2 = 4$: 3 in all. A small failing case like this names the bug in seconds.

items.title: Which of two problems first
items.prose: A problem worth $v$ points loses $v/250$ points every minute until you solve it, and neither problem here reaches its floor. P is worth 900. Q is worth 1,500 and takes you 45 minutes. You solve both, one after the other, starting at minute 0.
items.question: For what solving time of P, in minutes, do the two orders score the same?

feedback.correct: At 27 minutes P earns $900 / 27 = 33.3$ points a minute, the same as Q's $1500 / 45$.
feedback.generic: Swapping the two moves a loss of $v_Q t_P / 250$ against $v_P t_Q / 250$. Set them equal.

byKey.inverted: You inverted the ratio. The orders tie when $900 / t_P$ equals $1500 / 45$.
byKey.same: Equal times are not the break-even. Q is worth more, so P must be quicker to tie.

explain.text: P first costs Q $6 t_P$ points, and Q first costs P $3.6 \cdot 45 = 162$. They tie when $6 t_P = 162$, at $t_P = 27$ minutes. Both orders then score 1,870.8, and if P takes less than 27 minutes it goes first.

items.title: A compounding sum modulo a prime
items.prose:
**Problem.** A position grows by a factor $g$ each day. The total of the first $n$ daily factors is $1 + g + g^2 + \dots + g^{n-1}$. Print it modulo $p = 10^9 + 7$.

Here $1 \le n \le 10^{18}$ and $0 \le g < p$. A term $g^0$ counts as 1, even when $g = 0$.
items.question: Complete `growth_sum(g, n)`.

widget.starter:
MOD = 10**9 + 7


def growth_sum(g, n):
    """Return 1 + g + g^2 + ... + g^(n-1) modulo MOD."""
    ...
widget.solution:
MOD = 10**9 + 7


def growth_sum(g, n):
    """Return 1 + g + g^2 + ... + g^(n-1) modulo MOD."""
    if g % MOD == 1:
        return n % MOD            # every term is 1
    top = (pow(g, n, MOD) - 1) % MOD
    return top * pow(g - 1, MOD - 2, MOD) % MOD
widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests. They cover small sums, $g = 0$, $g = 1$ (which divides by zero) and $g = p - 1$. One has $n = 10^6$ and four have $n$ near $10^{18}$. A loop over $n$ would need $10^{18}$ steps and is stopped at the 5 s limit.

feedback.correct: Closed form, one `pow` for the power and one for the inverse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 has $g = 1$. The closed form divides by $g - 1 = 0$, which has no inverse; the sum is just $n$.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has $g = p - 1$, which is $-1$ modulo $p$. The sum $1 + (-1)$ is 0, so keep every step reduced.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 is an ordinary case. Multiply by the inverse of $g - 1$; floor division after reducing gives a different number.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has $n = 10^6$. Reduce after the subtraction, and multiply by the inverse of $g - 1$, not divide.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 has $g = 1$ and $n = 10^{18}$. Return $n \bmod p$ without any loop.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 has $n = 10^{18}$. A loop over $n$ cannot finish; use the closed form with `pow(g, n, MOD)`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Read the last line of the message under the editor.

explain.text: The sum is $(g^n - 1)/(g - 1)$, and division modulo a prime is multiplication by $(g - 1)^{p-2}$. Both powers take $O(\log)$ multiplications, even for $n = 10^{18}$. When $g \equiv 1$ the inverse does not exist, and every term is 1, so the answer is $n \bmod p$.

items.title: Fewest delivery vans
items.prose:
**Problem.** A courier has $n$ orders with weights $w_i$ ($1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, $1 \le w_i \le 10^9$). A van carries one or two orders, and their total weight may not exceed `cap`. Every order alone weighs at most `cap`.

Find the fewest vans that carry every order.
items.question: Complete `fewest_vans(weights, cap)`.

widget.prelude:
import random as _rnd


def _weights(n, hi, seed):
    g = _rnd.Random(seed)
    return [g.randint(1, hi) for _ in range(n)]
widget.starter:
def fewest_vans(weights, cap):
    """A van takes one or two orders, total at most
    cap. Return the fewest vans."""
    ...
widget.solution:
def fewest_vans(weights, cap):
    """A van takes one or two orders, total at most
    cap. Return the fewest vans."""
    w = sorted(weights)
    i, j = 0, len(w) - 1
    vans = 0
    while i <= j:
        if i < j and w[i] + w[j] <= cap:
            i += 1                # the lightest rides with the heaviest
        j -= 1                    # the heaviest always leaves
        vans += 1
    return vans
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: six hand cases, including heavy orders that ride alone, then two with 200,000 orders. Matching every order against every other needs about $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ steps and is stopped at the 5 s limit. Answers are compared exactly.

feedback.correct: Sort, then pair the heaviest with the lightest when they fit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 shows a shortcut that fails: pairing neighbours, in input order or in sorted order, wastes room.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 breaks pairing in input order. Sort first, so the heaviest order is matched on purpose.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has orders that all pair up exactly. Check that your last van is counted.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has orders too heavy to share. Each needs its own van, and the loop must still end.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has 200,000 orders. Sort once and use two pointers; searching for a partner each time is too slow.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Read the last line of the message under the editor.

explain.text: The heaviest order must ride, and if anything can join it, the lightest can. So pair them when they fit, and otherwise send the heaviest alone. Sorting and two pointers make that $O(n \log n)$.

items.title: Largest set of compatible strategies
items.prose:
**Problem.** A desk has $n$ strategies ($1 \le n \le 16$). Some pairs conflict and cannot run together. The conflicts are given as pairs of strategy numbers from 0 to $n - 1$.

Find the size of the largest set of strategies that contains no conflicting pair.

items.title: Squares from a rectangle
items.prose: A trading floor of 47 by 30 tiles is split into square desks. Each cut removes the largest square that fits at one end of what is left, until nothing is left.
items.question: How many squares does it make?

feedback.correct: Squares of side 30, 17 and 13, then three of 4 and four of 1: 10 in all.
feedback.generic: Each cut is one subtraction in Euclid's algorithm. Count how many times each side fits.

byKey.steps: 5 is the number of division steps in Euclid's algorithm. A quotient of 3 or 4 stands for several squares.
byKey.moves: You subtracted 1 from the sum of the quotients. The last 1 by 1 piece is a square too.
byKey.gcd: 1 is the side of the smallest square, the gcd. The question asks how many squares.

explain.text: $47 = 1 \cdot 30 + 17$, $30 = 1 \cdot 17 + 13$, $17 = 1 \cdot 13 + 4$, $13 = 3 \cdot 4 + 1$ and $4 = 4 \cdot 1$. Each quotient counts the squares of one size, so there are $1 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 4 = 10$. The last side is 1, the gcd.

items.title: A delta-neutral book
items.prose:
**Problem.** A desk wants a book of $n$ positions ($1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$). The sizes must be $n$ different non-zero whole numbers of lots. Each lies between $-n$ and $n$, and they sum to 0.

Print any such book. If none exists, print nothing (return `None`).
items.question: Complete `neutral_book(n)`. Any valid book is accepted.

widget.starter:
def neutral_book(n):
    """Return n different non-zero integers in
    [-n, n] that sum to 0, or None if impossible."""
    return []  # replace this
widget.solution:
def neutral_book(n):
    """Return n different non-zero integers in
    [-n, n] that sum to 0, or None if impossible."""
    if n == 1:
        return None
    book = []
    k = 1
    if n % 2 == 1:
        book = [1, 2, -3]         # one triple absorbs the odd position
        k = 4
    for _ in range((n - len(book)) // 2):
        book += [k, -k]
        k += 1
    return book

tests.call: all(check_book(n, neutral_book(n)) for n in range(1, 121))

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. A checker accepts any valid book, so your pattern need not match ours. Tests 1 to 5 use $n = 1, 2, 3, 5, 8$. Test 6 tries every $n$ up to 120, and tests 7 and 8 use 199,999 and 200,000. A search over candidate lists is stopped at the 5 s limit.

feedback.correct: Pairs of opposite sizes handle even $n$; one triple absorbs the odd position.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: For $n = 1$ the only non-zero size within $\pm 1$ is $\pm 1$, which cannot sum to 0. Return `None`.
byKey.test-3: For $n = 3$ pairs alone leave one position. Try $1, 2, -3$.
byKey.test-4: For $n = 5$ use a triple that sums to 0 and one pair: $1, 2, -3, 4, -4$.
byKey.test-6: Some $n$ below 120 fails. Check the smallest one: the pattern for odd $n$ needs at least three positions.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has $n = 199{,}999$. Build the list directly from a pattern; searching cannot finish.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Read the last line of the message under the editor.

explain.text: Pairs $k, -k$ sum to 0 and use two positions each, so even $n$ is done. For odd $n$ at least three positions are needed, and $1 + 2 + (-3) = 0$ absorbs one, then pairs $\pm 4, \pm 5, \dots$ finish. Only $n = 1$ fails, since $\pm 1$ cannot sum to 0 alone.

items.title: Reviewing a round
items.prompt:
Your rating is 1,250. In a 120-minute round your log reads:

- A (rated 800): accepted at minute 8.
- B (rated 1,100): accepted at minute 33, after two wrong answers on test 2.
- C (rated 1,300, with $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$): opened at minute 41. You wrote a double loop, got "time limit exceeded on test 9" and patched it until the end. No accept.
- D: never opened. The final scoreboard showed 2,300 solves for D and 600 for C.

Afterwards you read C's editorial, agreed with it and closed the tab.

(a) Name three mistakes in the round, each with a rule that would have prevented it.

(b) What did C's constraints tell you before you wrote any code?

(c) Describe how you upsolve C, and when you redo it.

(d) What goes in your mistakes log, and how does it feed the next round?
items.model:
**(a)** Three mistakes, each with a rule.

- *No time cap on C.* You spent 79 minutes there, from minute 41 to 120. Rule: with no new idea after about 15 to 20 minutes, switch problems. The minutes already spent are gone.
- *D was never read.* The scoreboard showed 2,300 solves for D and 600 for C. Rule: read every statement first, then order by solves and by points per minute.
- *Resubmitting B without a hand case.* Two wrong answers on test 2 cost two penalties. Rule: after a wrong answer, reread the statement against the code and run a small hand-made case before submitting again.

**(b)** With $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, a double loop does about $(2 \cdot 10^5)^2 / 2 = 2 \cdot 10^{10}$ steps. That is far over about $10^8$ for the time limit. The constraints said to aim for $O(n \log n)$ or $O(n)$: a sort, a two-pointer pass or a dict. The verdict on test 9 was the large test saying the same thing. Patching a quadratic loop could not fix it.

**(c)** C is rated 1,300, only 50 above your 1,250. That is well inside the window of about 300 above your rating. Take the idea from the editorial, then close it. Write the code from scratch until it is accepted, with a size test of 200,000 values. Redo the problem cold a week later. Reading the editorial and nodding does not count as solving it.

**(d)** One line per mistake: the problem, the category and the rule. Here: C, "no time cap", switch after 20 minutes. D, "statements unread", read all and check the scoreboard. B, "no hand case", test before resubmitting. Read the log before the next round and in the first minutes of it. A 1,400 rating is a fair first-year target. Cutting these three mistakes is worth more than learning a new trick.

rubric.text: Names the unbounded time on C (about 79 minutes) and gives a cap or switch rule.
Names the unread problem D, citing the scoreboard (2,300 solves), with the rule to read every statement first.
Names the resubmitted wrong answers on B and the hand-case or reread rule.
Reads the constraints: $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ rules out $O(n^2)$ (about $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ steps) and points to $O(n \log n)$ or $O(n)$.
Upsolves C: takes the idea, closes the editorial and codes it from scratch. Notes C is within 300 of the rating.
Redoes it a week later. Keeps a mistakes log (problem, category, rule) read before the next round.

explain.text: A round review looks for process mistakes, not only the missing idea. The three here are a missing time cap, a skipped statement and a rushed resubmission. Each has a rule you can follow next week, and the log keeps you honest.
